title: BlackRock's Robert Mitchnick on the launch of the firm's staked ether ETF
transcript_text: So, this product adds yield on top of spot ether exposure. Does that make ether easier to position as a true portfolio allocation rather than a more volatile satellite trade? Well, I think it's definitely an attract development for investors. I think fundamentally the portfolio allocation decision is going to consider a lot of factors. And it is a little bit of a different equation today still for Bitcoin versus say ether where Bitcoin has this digital gold emerging monetary alternative type nature to it whereas Ethereum is very clearly a technology centric bet around blockchain innovation in the various use cases of ether and digital assets. So I think that it's going to continue to be looked at, you know, more consistent with tech and even venture equity type allocations. But for a lot of investors being able to capture some additional yield I think is a significant point of attraction. Yeah, and to your point for a long time, the ETF wrapper has been about giving investors simple price exposure to crypto. Does bringing staking into the structure mark a real shift from access products to products designed to capture the economics of the network itself? Yeah, I think that's a great way of framing it. In some respects, we think about what the ETPs did for Bitcoin. That was pretty close to silver bullet for a lot of investors in terms of being able to access Bitcoin in a super convenient turnkey accessible low cost way. It wasn't quite the same for the original ETPs and ether because you didn't have the staking yield capture as part of it. So obviously there was tremendous resonance to the initial launch of the ether ETPs as well. And ETHA was the third fastest ETF in history to reach 10 billion in AUM after IBID and FBTC. But they did have this limitation. And so now with staking in it, it becomes much closer like the Bitcoin ETPs were to a silver bullet for a lot of investors in terms of a super convenient exposure vehicle. One of the biggest questions around crypto ETFs is whether they're simply following demand or beginning to shape price discovery themselves. As more money moves into regulated crypto funds, how much do those flows start to influence the underlying market? Well, it's certainly been a factor that's where a lot of investors have been going to for their preferred exposure vehicle in this space. We've seen that across direct investors, across financial advisors, across institutional investors. So it's certainly a factor. I think what's really notable, and there's been some confusion in various corners of the internet about this, is how resilient those flows have been. And how disproportionately long-term by and hold fundamental type investors, we've seen in these products, you take Bitcoin and IBID for instance. Bitcoin down almost 50% obviously from its all-time high that it made in October, the flows in IBID on a year-to-date basis are actually slightly positive. So it could have been a lot of selling pressure elsewhere in the Bitcoin ecosystem on crypto exchanges, on these offshore levered perps platforms. But the ETF investor base has taken a much steadier longer-term fundamental view of things. ETFs have become a major bridge for investors who want crypto exposure without holding the asset directly. One of the inflow patterns told you so far about who's buying these products and whether that demand is strategic and long-term rather than speculative. Yeah, I would say that the retail contingent actually are some of the most long-term focused that we've seen, and they've tended to opportunistically buy the dips. The only part of the demand base where we do see some tendency towards short-termism is the roughly 10% or so percent that is actually comprised of hedge funds. And so what a lot of hedge funds are running is a separate strategy where they're taking advantage of a basis trade going along the ETF and short futures. And that's ultimately neutral in terms of its impact to Bitcoin's price, but it shows up in flows where it tends to generate some additional inflows in times where that basis gets wider. When the basis compresses, which can coincide with negative price moves, it looks like there's dollars flowing out of the ETFs and the hedges unwound. But the other kind of 90 plus percent of the investor base where they're talking about retail direct investors or talk about financial advisors, talking about other institutional investors, have tended to be very steady and have been on an accumulation path pretty consistently. So look at 2025, the number of the top inflowing ETFs in the world that had negative price return, the top 20, there was only one, which is IBIT. So despite negative price moves in Bitcoin, IBIT was fourth in the world in inflows with 26 billion in. So we've just seen that steady accumulation pattern on a long-term basis. What have crypto fund flows revealed about investor appetite for assets beyond Bitcoin? I mean, as you said, IBIT has just had this blockbuster debut and continues to be the leader among the spot Bitcoin ETFs. But are you seeing growing conviction around ether specifically, or is that still a much earlier story? Those are clearly the two assets that we see the most interesting. I think when you look at this space, Bitcoin is the clear number one, obviously it's roughly 60 percent of the entire market share of the whole space. Ether is a clear number two, it's low teens percent market share. The next is, you know, talking three, three, four percent market share. And so that's where overwhelmingly the interest we see is, but we do see pockets of interest in some of the other assets as well. And we continue to evaluate those as as conditions evolved and as maturity liquidity scale and use cases develop. But we take a very discerning approach in terms of what we would put in an I shares ETF. Zooming out, do you see the next chapter of crypto ETFs being more about sophisticated structures like staking or is the bigger story here? Still simply that regulated fund wrappers are bringing a new class of investors into the industry. Well, I think it's both. We're super excited about ETHB having launched now. We think it's going to resonate as the predominant vehicle for investors seeking convenient ether exposure within an ETF. But we also believe that something like IBIT, which was more plain vanilla structure is going to continue to be a very significant force in this space. And the vehicle of choice is it's been for a significant subset of the investing population. Well, we see some more exotic structures coming to this space. I think no question. Some of those will be interesting. Some of them will resonate with investors. We've continued to and we will take a discerning approach in thinking about where else we would expand in this space.
